$doc: Vyomi capability registry — Compute Engine. One entry per console section; level per substrate (nano = shared core, also dev_server/unified ingress; offline = appliance). Proven by tests/conformance/test_capabilities.py — a claim the backend does not honour fails CI.

gcp.compute.instances.crud.title: VM instances (create, start, stop, suspend, resume, reset, delete)

gcp.compute.instances.nano_vm.title: SSH (in-browser VM on Nano)
limitations: On Nano (in-browser VMs turned on) a Compute Engine instance is a real Linux VM running inside the browser tab (v86, 32-bit x86 Alpine, not the boot image you picked): the SSH section shows its boot state, an xterm.js shell on the VM serial console (root, no tunnel needed) and an ssh command that works only through the local vyomi-tunnel (>= 1.1.0) while the tab is open. Limits: 32-bit x86 only; the VM's RAM is its disk (Stop saves it, Terminate/Delete discards it); a background tab runs the VM several times slower; no general internet egress (only plain-HTTP URLs that allow CORS), so git clone / apt / pip from the internet do not work; the 21 MB image and 2 MB engine load on first launch only. With in-browser VMs off the section offers a Turn on in-browser VMs button and the instance stays a record. Offline uses the Docker-backed SSH described under gcp.compute.instances.data_plane.

gcp.compute.instances.data_plane.title: Guest OS access (SSH, screenshot, OS info)
limitations: SSH (offline): the instance is a real Docker container with sshd. Setting the `ssh-keys` metadata (POST /api/gcp/compute/instances/{id}/ssh-keys, USERNAME:KEY lines) creates the user and authorizes the key in the guest the way the guest agent does, so `ssh -i key user@host -p port` really logs in; malformed lines are rejected. OS info (GET .../os-info) is read from the running guest (os-release, kernel, arch, memory, uptime). OS Login keys use the same path. On Nano, OS info and Screenshot are not simulated; SSH is served by the in-browser VM (see gcp.compute.instances.nano_vm).
Screenshot: getScreenshot needs a real virtual display's framebuffer; none is rendered, so there is nothing to capture.
OS info: getGuestAttributes is populated by a guest agent writing back through the metadata server after boot; no guest OS or agent runs to report hostname, OS release or kernel version.

gcp.compute.instances.serial_console.title: Serial port output
limitations: Serial output is Vyomi's own instance lifecycle record (create/start/stop/suspend/resume/reset, each at its real timestamp) rendered as console lines, not a real guest kernel's boot/console text — no guest OS runs to produce authentic kernel or init messages.

gcp.compute.images.crud.title: Custom images (create from disk, import rawDisk from Cloud Storage, export to Cloud Storage, import/export history)
limitations: Import (images.insert with rawDisk.source) really checks the .tar.gz object exists in the simulator's Cloud Storage; export writes an image archive (tar.gz with image metadata) into a real destination bucket object. Disk CONTENTS are not modeled, so neither moves guest bytes.

Export, and the import/export history (global/imageJobs), are Vyomi collections: real gcloud compute images import|export run Cloud Build workflows and show up as Cloud Build history, which Vyomi does not run.

gcp.compute.instance_groups.crud.title: Instance groups (unmanaged and managed)
limitations: Autoscaling policies aren't simulated — there's no real request load for a policy to react to, so resize (manual, or a rolling update's own batch of creates/deletes) is the only way the member count changes.

gcp.compute.vm-manager.title: VM Manager (Patch, OS policies, OS inventory, reports, VM extension policies)
limitations: The OS Config control plane is real: patch jobs (instance filters over the real Compute instances, validation, cancel, per-instance details), patch deployments (schedules, pause/resume, due runs create real patch jobs), OS policy assignments, VM extension policies, OS inventory (instances.inventories) and a fleet patch report.

Offline, a patch job on a running VM with metadata enable-osconfig=TRUE really runs the package manager (apt-get/yum/dnf/apk) inside the instance container via docker exec and reports its exit status; OS inventory is read from the live container (os-release, uname, dpkg/rpm/apk). On Nano there is no guest: patch jobs report SUCCEEDED having changed nothing and inventory is only the OS declared by the boot image (vyomiSource IMAGE_DECLARED, no packages).

A running VM without enable-osconfig=TRUE is NO_AGENT_DETECTED; a stopped VM is INACTIVE. OS policy assignments are recorded and report rolloutState SUCCEEDED but are never enforced and there is no per-VM compliance; VM extension policies are not installed. Patch jobs settle on a short wall-clock timer; pre/post patch steps are validated, never executed.

gcp.compute.observability.title: Observability, recommendations and VM Manager
limitations: The status duration and recent-activity feed shown here are real — Vyomi's own recorded instance lifecycle operations (insert/start/stop/suspend/resume/reset/...) at their real timestamps — not Cloud Monitoring charts or Cloud Logging entries: there's no request-metering engine tying a VM's real CPU/disk/network state to a sampled time series (the same boundary as gcp.storage.observability).
Recommender suggestions are state-derived (see gcp.compute.recommender), not Google's usage-based AI insights.
VM Manager is modelled as a control plane only (see gcp.compute.vm-manager): no guest agent runs, so nothing is applied to the VM.

gcp.compute.recommender.title: Recommender (Compute Advisor, dashboard recommendations)
limitations: Recommendations are computed from live Compute state only (unattached disks, in-use disks without any backup, unused reservations, unattached resource policies, empty sole-tenant node groups). There is no CPU/memory/network utilisation telemetry, so Google's usage-based recommenders (idle VM, rightsizing machine type) are not produced.
Idle-disk recommendations fire immediately on an unattached disk; the real recommender observes it for ~14 days first. Savings are estimates from list prices, not your billing data.
Applying a recommendation is manual: markClaimed/markSucceeded/markFailed/markDismissed record state, nothing is auto-remediated.

gcp.compute.instance_schedules.title: Instance schedules (scheduled VM start/stop)
limitations: Schedules are evaluated lazily on every Compute API call (no background thread in a substrate-independent core): fire times missed while the appliance/browser tab was not running are caught up (last 24 snapshot fires, the most recent start/stop) at the next call instead of firing at their wall-clock minute.
Time zones need the host's tz database; on a runtime without one (some in-browser Python builds) schedules evaluate in UTC.

gcp.compute.snapshot_schedules.title: Snapshot schedules (hourly / daily / weekly with retention)
limitations: Schedules are evaluated lazily on every Compute API call (no background thread in a substrate-independent core): fire times missed while the appliance/browser tab was not running are caught up (last 24 snapshot fires, the most recent start/stop) at the next call instead of firing at their wall-clock minute.
Scheduled snapshots are metadata records (size is the disk's provisioned size, not changed blocks); there is no incremental block storage to snapshot.
Application-consistent (guest flush) snapshots need a guest agent; `guestFlush` is stored but not honoured.

gcp.compute.instant_snapshots.title: Instant snapshots
limitations: Instant snapshots are zonal metadata records of a disk (name, source, size); no block data is captured, so a restored disk is an empty disk of the same size.

gcp.compute.async_replication.title: Disk async replication
limitations: Replication pairing, constraints (cross-region, size, unattached secondary) and lifecycle are real, but disks hold no block data here, so nothing is copied and there is no measured RPO/replication lag; state is always ACTIVE until stopped.

gcp.compute.consistency_groups.title: Disk consistency groups
limitations: A consistency group is a diskConsistencyGroupPolicy resource policy attached to disks; group-wide crash-consistent snapshotting and group failover are not performed because no block data is replicated.

gcp.compute.instances.multi_nic.title: Multiple network interfaces
limitations: Up to 8 NICs in distinct VPC networks are stored and returned (nic0..nicN, per-NIC internal IP); packet forwarding between NICs and per-NIC routing are not simulated (no guest network stack).

gcp.compute.instances.lb_health_check_fi.title: Load balancer health-check firewall rule
limitations: The console creates a real VPC firewall rule (130.211.0.0/22, 35.191.0.0/16 on the chosen ports, target tag lb-health-check) and tags the instance; there is no load balancer sending health probes.

gcp.compute.network_endpoint_groups.title: Network endpoint groups
limitations: Zonal, global (internet) and regional serverless NEGs with endpoint attach/detach/list and validation are real; endpoint health is not reported and a NEG cannot be attached to a backend service because no load balancer data plane exists.

gcp.compute.reservations.title: Reservations
limitations: Capacity is not actually held back: reservations are accounting. Running VMs whose machine type and zone match (and whose reservationAffinity allows it) are counted as consumers up to the reserved count, but a VM is never refused for lack of unreserved capacity.
Shared reservations (shareSettings) are stored, not enforced across projects.

gcp.compute.sole_tenant.title: Sole-tenant nodes (node templates, node groups, node types)
limitations: Node groups, templates and VM-to-node placement (first-fit by vCPU and memory, with a hard fit check at VM creation) are real; there is no physical host, so maintenance policies and autoscaling are stored but never act, and CPU overcommit is not modelled.

gcp.compute.storage_pools.title: Hyperdisk Storage Pools
limitations: Pool capacity accounting (a disk can't exceed free provisioned capacity; ADVANCED allows 5x thin provisioning) and disk-type matching are enforced; provisioned IOPS/throughput are stored but disks are not throttled by them (there is no I/O path).

gcp.compute.rollouts.title: Rollouts
limitations: Compute rollout plans orchestrate Google-managed product updates across waves; there is no managed fleet or update stream to roll out.

gcp.compute.security-risk-overview.title: Security risk overview
limitations: Compute findings are a deterministic rule engine over stored VMs/firewalls. Threat findings come from Vyomi's deterministic detector over the control-plane calls the simulator served (bucket opened to allUsers, Owner/Editor granted, log sink deleted, world-open firewall, KMS destruction, service-account key creation) - no ML threat analysis and no attack-path simulation. Image vulnerabilities come from Artifact Registry scanning (core/vuln_scan_core.py: bundled advisory snapshot + EOL table over the image config; the real Trivy container where the offline appliance has it). It is not Security Command Center: no findings history, muting or org-level aggregation.

gcp.compute.migrate-to-vms.title: Migrate to Virtual Machines (sources, connectors, migrating VMs, replication cycles, clone/cutover jobs)
limitations: The vmmigration v1 control plane is real: sources (VMware/AWS/Azure with validation, credentials never echoed), datacenter connectors, migrating VMs with the READY -> FIRST_SYNC -> ACTIVE -> PAUSED/CUTOVER -> FINALIZED state machine, replication cycles, clone jobs and cutover jobs (preconditions enforced), long-running operations. Clone and cutover create a REAL Compute Engine instance (visible in VM instances, offline as a Compute-store record).

Replication is record-only: no disk bytes are copied and there are no source hypervisors, so the VM inventory is declared by you (vyomiInventory on the source). The created Compute Engine instance boots a stock image, not the source VM's disks. Replication cycles are generated from the wall clock (first sync about 2 s, then one cycle per 30 s).

gcp.compute.incidents.title: Google Cloud incidents (service health feed)
limitations: The feed reports outages on Google's real infrastructure; Vyomi is a local simulator with no Google status source, so there is nothing true to report.

gcp.compute.tpus.title: TPUs (Cloud TPU v2 nodes)
limitations: Record-level Cloud TPU v2 API: nodes create/get/list/patch/delete/start/stop with a CREATING -> READY state machine, accelerator-type and runtime-version catalogues that are zone-aware, and a per-zone, per-generation quota check (RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED). There is no accelerator: nothing can run on a TPU node. Queued resources and TPU pods' networking are not simulated.

gcp.compute.bms.title: Bare Metal Solution (servers, networks, VRFs, volumes, NFS shares, procurements, maintenance events)
limitations: Bare Metal Solution provisions physical Oracle-certified servers in a Google-colocated facility with procurement and on-site maintenance workflows; there is no hardware (or meaningful software stand-in) to model.

gcp.compute.committed-use-discounts.title: Committed use discounts (resource-based and spend-based commitments)
limitations: Commitments are real records: regionCommitments insert/get/list/aggregatedList with validation (plan, series, vCPU/memory ratio), 1-year/3-year terms, list discounts (37%/55% resource-based, 28%/46% spend-based) and ACTIVE/EXPIRED status from the term. Utilisation and net savings are real arithmetic over the RUNNING instances in the Compute store priced with the cost meter's GCP list prices (core/cost_model.py).

Nothing is billed and no Google billing account is involved. As on GCP a commitment cannot be cancelled (DELETE returns FAILED_PRECONDITION). Spend-based commitments use a Vyomi field vyomiSpend.hourlyCommitmentUsd (the real purchase is a Cloud Billing action). LICENSE commitments, reservations attached to commitments and auto-renewal behaviour are not simulated.

gcp.compute.capacity-advisor.title: Capacity advisor (quota, reservations, simulated fleet)
limitations: SIMULATED FLEET, NO GOOGLE FLEET DATA. Three tiers: (1) project quota per region for CPUS and the machine family (FAILED / QUOTA_EXCEEDED); (2) an active, unutilised matching reservation (GUARANTEED); (3) a dry-run allocation on a simulated fleet - zone = datacenter, 128-core/512 GB hosts, requested shape = VM, a deterministic per-zone background load that fluctuates over time (HIGH_PROBABILITY, LOW_PROBABILITY or ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED). The probe allocates then deallocates and never consumes capacity. The same pure-Python model runs on Nano and offline (the cloudsim-backbone JVM bridge is not used), so answers are identical for the same state and time.

Real instance inserts/starts/resumes draw from per-zone, per-machine-family vCPU pools (reservations hold capacity; stop/delete returns it) and fail with ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED when a pool is full. Default pools are large, so normal flows never stock out; shrink a pool (Vyomi verb POST vyomi/capacityPools) or raise the background load (POST vyomi/capacityScenario, off by default) to rehearse stockouts. Quota is advisory only (not enforced on insert).
Pool sizes, host shape and background load are Vyomi's own numbers, not Google's.

gcp.compute.preview-features.title: Preview features (opt-in to pre-GA Compute Engine features)
limitations: The catalog and enrollment are managed by Google per project and gate real backend rollouts; Vyomi has a single fixed feature set.

gcp.compute.opsagent_metrics.title: Instance Observability: Ops Agent host metrics
limitations: agent.googleapis.com cpu (cpu_state=used only), network and disk series measured inside the instance (cgroup + /proc counters) and pushed to /_obs/gce-counters by a runtime; there is no built-in sampler for GCE instances on this branch, so a VM with no pushes shows 'No samples'. Memory, process and filesystem metrics are not produced.

gcp.compute.instances.ssh_metadata.title: SSH keys and OS info
limitations: SSH keys: the instance `ssh-keys` metadata item (and the project one) is real state: lines are validated as USERNAME:ssh-key, shown with SHA256 fingerprints, block-project-ssh-keys is honoured in the effective list. Offline, saving authorizes each key inside the running instance container (guest-agent behaviour) so `ssh -i key user@host -p port` logs in; removing a line does not yet revoke the key already written to the guest. On Nano the metadata is recorded and validated but no guest receives it (SSH there is the in-browser VM).
OS info: offline it is read from the running guest (os-release, uname, /proc); on Nano, or when the instance is stopped, it is declared from the boot image only (no kernel, uptime or package counts).
OS Login (IAM-based key distribution) is not simulated: the `enable-oslogin` flag is shown but identity-based login is not enforced.
